aristotle: Aristotle (384–322 BC), a Greek philosopher who studied under Plato and tutored Alexander the Great, covered nearly every field of knowledge, from biology to logic. In ethics he argued that the good life is eudaimonia — flourishing through virtuous action guided by practical wisdom, with virtue as a mean between extremes.
berkeley: George Berkeley (1685–1753) was an Anglo-Irish bishop and empiricist philosopher famous for denying that matter exists apart from perception: for him, to be is to be perceived (esse est percipi), with everything existing only in minds, including God's.
descartes: René Descartes (1596–1650), a French mathematician and philosopher often called the father of modern philosophy, used radical doubt to reach his famous conclusion 'I think, therefore I am' (the cogito). His sharp distinction between mind and body shaped centuries of debate about consciousness.
gilligan: Carol Gilligan (born 1936) is an American psychologist and ethicist whose 1982 book In a Different Voice challenged Lawrence Kohlberg's model of moral development, arguing that care and responsibility in relationships constitute a distinct moral voice alongside, not below, the logic of rights and justice.
heidegger: Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) was a German philosopher whose Being and Time reoriented twentieth-century thought around the question of what it means to be. His analyses of authenticity, anxiety, death, and 'the they' proved hugely influential — complicated, for many readers, by his involvement with Nazism.
kant: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), the central figure of the German Enlightenment, argued that morality is grounded in reason rather than consequences: his categorical imperative demands that we act only on principles we could will as universal laws, and never treat persons merely as means.
kierkegaard: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855), a Danish writer often called the father of existentialism, wrote pseudonymously about anxiety, despair, and the passionate 'leap of faith' required for genuine religious commitment, insisting that the deepest truths must be lived subjectively rather than merely grasped objectively.
laozi: Laozi, a shadowy figure traditionally dated to the sixth century BC and regarded as the author of the Tao Te Ching, is credited as the founder of Taoism. His central ideas are the Tao — the ineffable Way underlying all things — and wu wei, effortless, non-coercive action.
marx: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was a German philosopher, economist, and revolutionary whose 'historical materialism' holds that economic structures shape society, politics, and ideas. His analyses of alienation, class struggle, and commodity fetishism made him one of modernity's most consequential — and contested — thinkers.
mill: John Stuart Mill (1806–1873), a British philosopher and liberal reformer, refined utilitarianism — the view that right actions maximize happiness — by distinguishing higher from lower pleasures, and in On Liberty defended individual freedom with his harm principle: society may restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others.
nietzsche: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and provocateur who declared that 'God is dead' and asked what values could survive that loss. His ideas — the Übermensch, will to power, master and slave morality, eternal recurrence — have influenced philosophy, literature, and pop culture alike.
noddings: Nel Noddings (1929–2022) was an American philosopher of education and a leading voice of the ethics of care, arguing that caring relations — being received and responded to by another — are the foundation of morality rather than abstract rules or principles.
nozick: Robert Nozick (1938–2002) was an American philosopher whose Anarchy, State, and Utopia defended a minimal state and challenged redistributive theories of justice. He also posed the famous 'experience machine' thought experiment, asking whether we would plug into a device guaranteeing only pleasant experiences.
parmenides: Parmenides (c. 515–450 BC) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Elea who argued, in dense verse, that what truly is must be one, eternal, and unchanging — so the changing world our senses report is an illusion. This radical claim set the agenda for much of Western metaphysics.
plato: Plato (428–348 BC) was a Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and founder of the Academy, whose dialogues shaped Western thought. His Theory of Forms, allegory of the cave, and vision of justice in the Republic remain among philosophy's most enduring images.
putnam: Hilary Putnam (1926–2016) was an American philosopher who made major contributions across mind, language, and science. He devised the 'brain in a vat' skeptical scenario and the Twin Earth case, arguing that meanings depend on the world and community, not just on what is in the head.
quine: W.V.O. Quine (1908–2000) was a dominant figure in twentieth-century analytic philosophy who pictured our beliefs as a single web, adjusted as a whole against experience. His arguments for the indeterminacy of translation and against the analytic–synthetic distinction reshaped debates about language and knowledge.
rachels: James Rachels (1941–2003) was an American moral philosopher and textbook author who brought clear argument to applied questions — euthanasia, animal welfare, and moral relativism among them. His critique of ethical egoism and his work on the moral status of animals remain widely studied.
sartre: Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) was a French philosopher, novelist, and public intellectual, the leading voice of existentialism. He held that existence precedes essence — we have no fixed nature and are 'condemned to be free' — and that bad faith is the evasion of that freedom.
socrates: Socrates (470–399 BC), the Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, is known through Plato's dialogues: a relentless questioner who claimed to know only that he knew nothing and held that the unexamined life is not worth living. Condemned by an Athenian jury, he became philosophy's founding martyr.
thomson: Judith Jarvis Thomson (1929–2020) was an American moral philosopher best known for her 1971 'violinist' thought experiment, a landmark defense of the moral permissibility of abortion, and for developing the trolley problem, which has become central to debates about killing, letting die, and moral intuitions.
williams: Bernard Williams (1929–2003) was a British philosopher regarded by many as the sharpest critic of utilitarianism and of impartial 'moral theory' generally. His ideas of moral luck and of integrity — the objection that utilitarianism alienates people from their own projects — remain deeply influential.
wittgenstein: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), an Austrian-born philosopher who worked largely in Cambridge, transformed philosophy twice: first with the picture theory of the Tractatus, then with the later idea that meaning lies in 'language games' — public uses of words — including his famous private language argument.
zizek: Slavoj Žižek is a contemporary Slovenian philosopher and cultural critic who fuses Hegel, Marx, and Lacanian psychoanalysis to analyze ideology, exposing how popular culture and everyday life quietly encode political fantasy. His flamboyant style has made him one of the most recognizable living philosophers.
